n: A new collection begins (chapters 10–22:16): short, two-line sayings, most contrasting the wise and the foolish. The first is about family: a child’s choices bring joy or grief to parents.

f.g: A heading that starts the main collection of individual sayings.

n: Wealth gained by wickedness has no lasting value; righteousness is what truly saves.
The Lord will not let the righteous go hungry, but he pushes away the cravings of the wicked.
Lazy hands lead to poverty, but hard work brings wealth—a general principle of everyday life.

f.w: the hand of the diligent maketh rich

n: A sensible young person works hard during harvest; one who sleeps through it brings shame. Some opportunities only come at certain seasons.
Blessings rest on the righteous person’s head, but the mouth of the wicked hides violence.

f.w: violence covereth the mouth of the wicked

n: The righteous are remembered with blessing; the name of the wicked rots away and is forgotten.

f.w: The memory of the just is blessed

n: The wise welcome instruction, but a babbling fool comes to ruin.
Integrity gives a secure path; crooked dealings eventually come to light.
A sly wink—a sign of deceit—causes trouble, and the babbling fool falls. The second line repeats verse 8; sayings were sometimes reused in different collections.

f.w: He that winketh with the eye

n: The words of the righteous refresh others like a spring of fresh water; the words of the wicked hide violence.
Hatred stirs up quarrels, but love covers over offenses. Both Peter and James echo this teaching.
Wisdom is heard on the lips of the discerning, but a rod is needed for the one without sense.

f.w: a rod is for the back

n: The wise store up knowledge, but a fool’s mouth invites disaster.

f.g: Treasure it, store it for later use.

n: An observation, not a moral judgment: wealth protects the rich like a fortified city, while poverty leaves the poor vulnerable.

f.g: A fortress—wealth acts as a protective wall.

n: The earnings of the righteous lead to life; what the wicked gain leads to more sin.
Accepting discipline keeps you on the road to life; refusing correction leads others (and yourself) astray.

f.g: erreth = goes astray, or causes others to go astray.

n: Hiding hatred behind lies and spreading slander both mark a fool.
The more you talk, the more likely you are to sin. Holding your tongue is wise.
A righteous person’s words are as valuable as fine silver; the thoughts of the wicked are nearly worthless.
The righteous nourish many with their words, but fools starve for lack of sense.

f.g: Like a shepherd feeding a flock.

n: The Lord’s blessing brings real wealth without the trouble that often comes with riches gained other ways.

f.w: he addeth no sorrow with it
f.g: Or “hard toil adds nothing to it.”

n: A fool enjoys wrongdoing like a game, but a person of understanding delights in wisdom.
What the wicked fear will happen to them; what the righteous long for will be given.

f.w: the desire of the righteous shall be granted

n: The wicked are swept away like a passing storm, but the righteous stand firm forever. Jesus told a similar parable of the wise and foolish builders.
A lazy messenger is as irritating as vinegar on the teeth or smoke in the eyes.

f.g: Those who send him on an errand.

n: Reverence for the Lord tends to lengthen life; wickedness tends to cut it short.
The hope of the righteous ends in joy, but the expectations of the wicked come to nothing.
The Lord’s way is a refuge for the upright but ruin for evildoers.
The righteous will never be uprooted; the wicked will not remain in the land.
The mouth of the righteous produces wisdom like a fruit tree; a perverse tongue will be cut off like a barren branch.
The righteous know what words are fitting; the wicked speak only what is twisted.
